1.pericope_label: No water at Rephidim; the rock in Horeb; Massah and Meribah

schools.summary: Settle the ground before settling the lesson, and be candid that the ground is unsettled. Three routes lead to the valley where most critics place Rephidim; reject the shortest, since it passes an Egyptian settlement a fugitive host would have avoided, and prefer the circuitous one because it is very open and therefore fit for a vast multitude. Note that the name means resting-places, which suits the most fertile spot in the peninsula, and note also that the brook there has been known to fail, so that the want of water is not incredible on the ground itself. Where a proposed site will not answer, say so rather than adopt it: rule out one too far from Sinai to be reached in a day, and rule out a spring whose valley is too narrow to hold a nation and whose well, never dry, answers neither to the thirst described nor to the rock in Horeb. Give the two names their roots, trial and quarrel, and let the etymology carry the sense rather than an application laid over it. And weigh the physical extremity honestly, since it governs how the chiding is read: water carried from Elim would by now be spent, children and cattle sharpened the need, and thirst kills more surely and quickly than hunger, whole armies having died of it and crews perished at sea with water on every side.

Refuse to excuse the murmuring, and set the offence in its sequence. Scarcely was the sedition about food quieted before this people rebelled about drink; had bread and water failed together they would have been the more excusable, but to murmur after being fed from heaven is intolerable perversity. Take the double charge of chiding and tempting as growing from one root, unbelief, and take the root of that to be ingratitude. Then press the test they failed, for it is the practical use of the passage: they knew well that fountains cannot be made by mortal men, so why quarrel with Moses rather than call upon God, when a spark of faith would have sent them to prayer? Do not pass over what the command cost Moses. The order to go out before the people was hard, since it exposed him to immediate danger, and it deserves remark that he neither trembled nor retreated; read the taking of the elders only as a middle course, which kept the glory of the miracle from being obscured while showing the multitude unworthy to witness it. And attend to the smaller words: the Lord standing on the rock stood there not as a spectator but to direct where the blow should fall.

Begin by putting the quarrel where it belongs. God was their leader, so all murmuring against Moses was reckoned against God, and no complaint against the servant stops at the servant. Then draw the mercy out of the instrument: the rod was carried this time not to summon a plague but to fetch water, and God maintains those who are at war with him, giving not merely a spring, as he showed one to Hagar, but water out of a rock. Ground the miracle where it can be examined. The rock was likely one Moses already knew from keeping Jethro's flocks; and the argument from what remains has weight, since the supply must have been vast to serve so great a host, which excludes artifice, and holes and channels are still shown in the stone. Then take the type on the apostle's authority, that the rock was Christ, and preach it with the warning the apostle himself attaches: many who drank of that rock perished notwithstanding. Let the hearer feel both halves. The water is free, sufficient and miraculous; the drinking of it saved nobody who went on tempting the God who gave it.

Begin where the difficulty actually begins, and do not begin later. They journeyed at the commandment of the Lord, led by the pillar, and came to a place where there was no water. Hold those two facts together and refuse to loosen either, for the whole lesson lies in their conjunction. A man may be in the way of his duty, going exactly where he was sent and guided visibly as he goes, and still meet with troubles; and those troubles are not evidence that he mistook the way. They are brought for the trial of his faith, and the trial is the point of them. Say this before saying anything about the murmuring, so that the hearer does not conclude that hardship in obedience is proof of disobedience. Then let the reproof fall, but let it fall on people whose difficulty has first been granted as real.

debates.question: Where did this happen, and which rock was struck?

sides.position: The route is uncertain; of three ways to the valley where most critics place Rephidim the shortest passes an Egyptian settlement they would have avoided, so the circuitous and very open road suits a vast host best, and the traditional rock is too far from Rephidim

No identification can be sustained: one proposed site lies too far from Sinai to be reached in a day, and another has a valley too narrow for a nation and a well that never runs dry, answering neither to the want of water nor to the rock in Horeb
The rock was one Moses already knew from keeping Jethro's flocks; the holes and channels still shown in the stone, and the volume required to supply so great a host, argue against artifice

Nearly so, given the extremity: water was scarce on that road, what they carried from Elim was spent, and children and cattle sharpened the need, so that nothing but a lively faith could have kept them patient; yet it was wrath and not faith that spoke

Not at all. Scarcely was the sedition about food quieted before they rebelled about drink; had bread and water failed together they would have been more excusable, but to murmur after being fed from heaven was intolerable perversity rooted in ingratitude
The question of degree is beside the point, since God was their leader and all murmuring against Moses was reckoned against God

outliers.note: Alone weighs the physiology of the danger, observing that thirst kills more surely and quickly than hunger, that whole armies have perished of it, and that crews have died at sea with water on every side and none to drink.

Alone spends the space refusing identifications rather than proposing one, ruling out a site too far from Sinai to be reached in a day and a spring whose valley is too narrow for a nation and whose well, never dry, answers neither to the want of water nor to the rock in Horeb.

themes: there was no water for the people to drink
I will stand before thee there upon the rock in Horeb; and thou shalt smite the rock
he called the name of the place Massah, and Meribah

8.pericope_label: Amalek fights Israel; Moses' hands stayed up by Aaron and Hur

schools.summary: Establish who Amalek was before asking why he came. The name marks descendants of Esau's grandson, and the tribe seems to have become the predominant people of the Sinaitic peninsula early; Balaam calls them the first of the nations, and though the Egyptian records do not name them, they were probably among the peoples constantly contending on the north-eastern frontier. Their expansion into so great a power by the Mosaic age is conceivable on the same pattern as the Edomites, who grew by absorbing the earlier population of Mount Seir. Then give the material cause its weight. They were near Sinai for the reason the Bedouin still leave the lower districts at the beginning of summer, because the grass dries below while the mountain pasture stays green; the Sinaitic region was their own summer and autumn ground, and in their absence a swarm of emigrants had occupied part of it and threatened the rest. Their hostility was therefore not altogether unprovoked, though the manner of it was pitiless. Introduce Joshua fully, since this is his first mention: an Ephraimite, tenth in descent from Joseph, about forty-five, still called Hoshea, probably already known for military capacity. And read the raised hand cautiously. It is not probable that the Israelites were affected by the movements, or could even discern them; it was Moses, Aaron and Hur who were struck by the coincidence, and the lesson taught was the value of intercessory prayer.

Do not take the descent for granted. There is a case that these Amalekites were not the posterity of Esau's grandson at all but descendants of Cush, in being long before that Amalek was born and bordering eastward on the wilderness of Shur; weigh it against the usual account rather than assuming the usual account. Then hold two causes of the war together. On the human side there was jealousy, the old grudge for the birthright and blessing transferred from Esau to Jacob, and an unwillingness that Jacob's posterity should enjoy the inheritance their ancestor lost. On God's side there was purpose: a people spared and indulged had waxed wanton in tranquillity, and war was sent to humble their pride and correct their idleness. On the raised hand, prefer the prayer gesture and give the reasons. Aben Ezra's objection to the banner reading has force, that Aaron or Hur would then have fixed the rod where it could be seen standing; and the Targums paraphrase the lifting of the hands as prayer. Then set aside the allegories, however plausible, that make Aaron and Hur the two Testaments and the stone Christ. There is more acuteness than solidity in them. The plain reason is enough: Moses mistrusted his own weakness, and therefore sought two assistants.

Take the attack as robbery before taking it as ancestral spite. The Amalekites fell on Israel as the wandering Arabs still fall on caravans in that desert, without provocation given and merely through hope of plunder; the baggage was the object, and the women, children, aged and infirm were killed because they were found with it. Then present Joshua as a type too evident to need pointing out, since the Septuagint and the Greek Testament alike render his name Jesus: he conquered the enemies of his people, brought them into the promised land, and divided it by lot. Set beside him the division of labour, that God qualifies his people for various services for the good of his church, Joshua fighting, Moses praying, and both ministering to Israel. On the hands, refuse a literal mechanism outright. Lifting or lowering them could not humanly influence a battle; the gesture is prayer, and it means two things, that help must come from God alone and that supplication is necessary to prevail. Then apply it inwardly and let the hearer test himself by it: while the soul exerts itself in prayer we conquer our spiritual adversaries, but if our hands become heavy, if we restrain prayer, Amalek prevails, and every internal corruption gains ground.

Read the war in both directions at once. It was Israel's affliction, and note the sequence: they had been quarrelling with Moses, and now God sends Amalekites to quarrel with them, for wars abroad are the just punishment of strifes and discontents at home. It was also Amalek's sin, an hereditary malice running in the blood, defying the power that had so lately ruined Egypt. Then make the rod do its double work. Moses held it up to Israel to animate them, a banner reminding the soldiers of the glorious things already wrought; and he held it up to God by way of appeal, is not the battle the Lord's? Note also that trust in God is not the opposite of using means: when the Egyptians pursued, Israel stood still, but now they must bestir themselves. Then draw the hardest lesson from the heavy hands. Joshua's hands were not heavy in fighting; Moses's were heavy in praying, and the more spiritual any service is, the more apt we are to fail and flag in it. Let the failure be met as it was met, by asking help, since we are members one of another. And end with the two figures together: Christ is our Joshua, the captain of our salvation who fights our battles, and our Moses, who ever lives making intercession that our faith fail not.

debates.question: Who were the Amalekites, and what moved them to attack?

sides.position: Descendants of Esau's grandson who had become the predominant people of the peninsula, and not wholly unprovoked: the Sinaitic region was their own summer and autumn pasture, occupied in their absence by emigrants who threatened to seize the rest

Descendants of Esau's grandson, grown great as the Edomites did by absorbing an earlier population, and near Sinai for the reason the Bedouin still leave the lower districts in summer for cooler grazing
Not the posterity of Esau's grandson at all, but descendants of Cush who were in being long before that Amalek was born
Hereditary malice: the old grudge over the birthright and blessing, running in the blood and sharpened as the promise moved toward its accomplishment
Plunder, and nothing ancestral: they fell on Israel as the wandering Arabs still fall on caravans in that desert, the baggage being the object
Two causes at once, their jealousy over the lost birthright and God's own purpose to humble a people grown wanton in tranquillity

debates.question: What was the raised hand doing?

sides.position: Both banner and appeal: the rod that had summoned the plagues was held up to animate the soldiers, and held up to God by way of pleading that the battle was his

Neither, so far as the army was concerned, since it is not probable they could even discern the movements; God varied the fortunes of the fight to teach the value of intercessory prayer, and it was the three men on the hill who were struck by the coincidence

Prayer, with no literal mechanism admitted, since lifting or lowering the hands could not humanly influence a battle; the gesture means that help comes from God alone and that supplication is necessary to prevail
Prayer, on the authority of the Targums; and Aben Ezra's objection tells against the banner reading, since Aaron or Hur would then have fixed the rod where it could be seen standing

outliers.note: Alone denies the Esau descent, making these Amalekites descendants of Cush who were in being long before Amalek the grandson of Esau, and bordering eastward on the wilderness of Shur.

Alone reports and sets aside the received allegories on the scene, that Aaron and Hur are the two Testaments on which prayer rests and the stone is Christ, judging them to have more acuteness than solidity, and resting instead on Moses' mistrust of his own weakness.

themes: Then came Amalek, and fought with Israel in Rephidim
when Moses held up his hand, that Israel prevailed: and when he let down his hand, Amalek prevailed
Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands, the one on the one side, and the other on the other side

14.pericope_label: The memorial in the book; the altar Jehovah-nissi; war with Amalek

schools.summary: Read the article in the Hebrew and let it carry historical weight. The text says in the book, not merely in a book, and that a book existed before Moses is implied by his own quotations and has been abundantly confirmed by Egyptian papyri dating from long before the Jewish lawgiver; the expression seems to imply a record already kept, in which God's dealings with his people were entered from time to time, probably the germ of the existing Pentateuch. Note honestly that the pointing which distinguishes the two readings rests on tradition alone. On the altar, observe that altars are otherwise not given special names, Jacob's being the exception, and that a name serves a memorial by keeping the event in remembrance; observe as well that nothing is said here about sacrifices being offered, so the altar with its expressive name may have been memorial and watchword rather than a place of offering. Do not force the banner back onto the rod: the banner is Jehovah himself, under whose protection Israel fought and conquered. On the last verse be exact about the difficulty. The unique word rendered throne is the real obstacle, and the ancient versions should be set out; yet the sense the margin gives is plain enough, that Amalek lifted his hand against the throne of God and God will therefore war with him from generation to generation. Trace the fulfilment through Saul and David to its completion in the reign of Hezekiah.

Do not spend the passage on the question of the book. The dispute about which book is meant is superfluous; God simply wills that the memory of this deliverance should never perish, and it does not perish, since Moses handed it down in writing to the end of the world together with the doctrine of the Law. Attend instead to why Joshua in particular must hear it read: he faced many difficulties, and nothing could support him with firmer resolve than knowing that Amalek, who first made war on Israel, was already condemned by divine decree and could not escape. Take the altar's purpose to be the people's, not the leader's. Moses did not erect a statue to God nor honour the altar by God's name for its own sake, but so that Israel, elated by success, should not boast of their own strength but glory only in God. Keep the word rendered banner as banner. On the closing verse set aside both the reading that makes it an oath, since it is not credible that God should swear by what Christ forbade, and the reading that makes the throne the Church. Take the hand upon the throne to mean that God does not sit idly in heaven as the Epicureans imagine, but exercises dominion, and while he reigns will never cease to pursue this nation with just vengeance.

Say plainly what is not known. This is the first mention of writing on record, and we cannot tell what it signified or how it was done; the command may have been given only after the law was written on tables of stone, and the memorial here may be some symbolic registration rather than alphabetical characters. Note the charge given in Joshua's hearing, which shows he was to succeed Moses, and that such a charge belongs to every succeeding governor. On the name, press the military figure. The hands and rod were held up as soldiers hold their standards; and since standards bear the arms of the country, so that men fight under that banner in its defence, the name of Jehovah became the armorial bearing of the whole congregation, each man feeling himself not his own but the Lord's soldier. Where the Hebrew of the last verse resists translation, show the reader the options rather than one rendering: the conjecture that throne is a copyist's error for ensign, the two letters being easily confused, and the suggestion that a hand holding a cup of wrath was carved on one of the altar stones. And close where the altar closes, that he who does all the work should have all the praise.

debates.question: What book is meant, and could such a record be written this early?

sides.position: The Hebrew has the book, and the definite article, with Egyptian papyri long anterior to Moses, implies a record already kept in which God's dealings were entered from time to time, probably the germ of the Pentateuch

This is the first mention of writing on record, and what it signified cannot be told; the verse may anticipate a later command, since the first regular alphabetical writing was likely that on the tables of stone, so some symbolic registration may be meant
The first mention of writing in scripture, and the command was perhaps not given until after the law was written on tables of stone
The dispute about the book is superfluous; God simply wills that the memory should never perish, and the narration of Moses effected that

debates.question: Were sacrifices offered on this altar?

sides.position: Primarily yes, as thank-offerings acknowledging the victory, with the memorial purpose secondary; the name was given because altars are otherwise unnamed and a name keeps the event in remembrance
Thank-offerings were offered there, or at least a monument was erected in memory of the victory
Nothing at all is said about sacrifices, so the altar with its expressive name may have served as memorial and watchword rather than as a place of offering

debates.question: Is the closing verse obscure, and what is the hand upon the throne?

sides.position: It can scarcely be called obscure; it plainly gives the sense placed in the margin, that Amalek lifted his hand against the throne of God and God will therefore war with him
Obscure, chiefly on account of the unique word rendered throne, which the ancient versions handle variously

The oath reading is reported from the Targum of Jonathan, Jarchi and Aben Ezra, but Drusius objects that God should not swear by what Christ forbade; the hand is rather Amalek's, against the throne among his people

Neither an oath nor the Church as throne: the hand upon the throne means that God does not sit idly in heaven as the Epicureans imagine, but exercises dominion, and while he reigns will pursue this nation with vengeance

The received text is at fault; throne is probably a copyist's error for ensign, the two Hebrew letters being easily confused, and another conjecture makes it a hand holding a cup of wrath carved on an altar stone

outliers.note: Alone leaves the received text, preferring the conjecture that throne is a copyist's error for ensign and reporting another that a hand holding a cup of wrath was carved on one of the altar stones.
Alone observes that nothing whatever is said about sacrifices being offered on this altar, and infers that it served as memorial and watchword to posterity rather than as a place of offering.

themes: Write this for a memorial in a book, and rehearse it in the ears of Joshua
Moses built an altar, and called the name of it Jehovah-nissi
the LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation
